items.article_text_original: Report highlights disease elimination milestones, progress in immunization and maternal health, and expanded access to medicines, while warning of the loss of the Region’s measles-free status and other health threats Washington, D.C., September 28, 2026 (PAHO) – The Director of the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, presented his Annual Report today at the opening of the 63rd Directing Council, highlighting important health gains across the Americas despite a complex public health environment and increasing financial constraints. Covering the period from July 2025 through June 2026, the report highlights progress in disease elimination, health security, immunization, maternal health, primary health care, access to essential medicines and health technologies, and the use of innovation to expand access to health services. “These achievements show what is possible when we work together and why we must continue to build on that progress,” said Dr Barbosa. Countries advance toward disease elimination Over the past year, countries and territories achieved important disease elimination milestones. Brazil and the Bahamas were validated as having eliminated mother-to-child transmission of HIV. Turks and Caicos Islands received certification for the elimination of mother-to-child transmission of HIV and became the first territory in the Americas to validate the elimination of mother-to-child transmission of hepatitis B. Chile became the first country in the Region to be verified as having eliminated leprosy, while five provinces in Argentina were confirmed free of vector-borne transmission of Chagas disease. “These milestones demonstrate what can be accomplished through sustained national commitment, with PAHO's support,” Dr. Barbosa said. The report also underscores the fragility of hard-won public health gains. During the reporting period, the Region lost its measles-free status after sustained transmission was reestablished in Canada. Yellow fever outbreaks in several countries, together with declining measles vaccination coverage, also highlighted the risk of setbacks against vaccine-preventable diseases. Strengthening health security and immunization Health security remained a central pillar of PAHO’s work. The Organization mobilized 174 tons of essential supplies to help countries prepare for and respond to disasters, complex humanitarian emergencies and disease outbreaks, and deployed experts and coordinated emergency medical teams during health emergencies. PAHO’s surveillance systems also analyzed more than 2.2 million signals related to potential public health events, supporting early detection and rapid response across the Region. Immunization also continued to recover from declines experienced before and during the COVID-19 pandemic. The number of unvaccinated children under 1 year old fell from 1.3 million to 1.1 million. However, declining measles vaccination coverage demonstrated the need to further strengthen routine immunization programs and increase vaccine uptake through effective communication and public education. Progress in maternal health Reducing preventable maternal deaths remained a priority across the Region. Of the 12 countries receiving targeted PAHO support, 10 recorded declines in maternal mortality ratios during the reporting period. Stronger surveillance systems, supportive policies, improvements in primary health care, and a strengthened health workforce contributed to these gains. Strengthening prevention and care for noncommunicable diseases PAHO expanded its work to prevent and control noncommunicable diseases, with primary health care continuing to serve as the foundation for prevention, early diagnosis and integrated care. By the end of the reporting period, PAHO’s HEARTS initiative was being implemented in more than 14,000 primary health care centers, reaching an estimated 50 million adults. The number of patients receiving treatment for hypertension increased by more than 20% in one year, from 5.7 million in 2025 to 6.9 million in 2026. The growing burden of mental health conditions also prompted new action, including the launch of PAHO’s Regional Suicide Prevention Initiative, which seeks to strengthen national policies and programs through multisectoral action tailored to countries’ needs and contexts. Regional solidarity expands access to medicines and vaccines PAHO’s Regional Revolving Funds continued to demonstrate the value of regional solidarity in improving equitable access to essential medicines and health technologies, supporting the procurement of more than 214 million vaccine doses, over 10 million diagnostic tests and more than 1 million treatments. The Funds also expanded their portfolio to include new high-price medicines, including treatments for breast and prostate cancer, multiple sclerosis and rare diseases. Through pooled procurement, countries were able to achieve significant price reductions. Innovation expands access to health services Innovation also contributed to progress across multiple areas of health. With PAHO’s technical cooperation, countries expanded the use of digital tools and adopted new approaches to address persistent public health challenges. More than 780 telehealth kits were distributed to 20 countries, bringing diagnosis, monitoring and clinical follow-up closer to populations that have historically faced barriers to access. Strengthening regional vaccine production During the reporting period, PAHO signed a landmark agreement with a global influenza vaccine manufacturer to secure a share of pandemic influenza vaccine production for countries in Latin America and the Caribbean. The agreement will support access to vaccines amid surging global demand in the event of a future pandemic. In parallel, PAHO reached a technology transfer agreement to strengthen regional production of seasonal influenza vaccines using cell-based platforms, helping modernize regional vaccine manufacturing and reduce dependence on external suppliers. “The achievements of the past year reflect the strength of our partnership with Member States and the power of regional solidarity,” Dr. Barbosa said. “Despite growing financial constraints, PAHO has once again demonstrated the resilience, adaptability, and leadership that have defined this Organization for more than 120 years.” Building on progress The report also highlights the challenges that remain, including aging populations, the growing burden of noncommunicable diseases, emerging and reemerging health threats, climate-related emergencies and persistent inequities. “Our work is far from finished,” Dr. Barbosa said. “Addressing these challenges will require sustained investment, stronger collaboration, and an unwavering commitment to solidarity.” Member States, with PAHO’s support, will continue working to build stronger health systems, protect public health gains, and ensure that the progress reflected in the report translates into lasting improvements in the lives of people across the Americas. LINKS Coverage of the 63rd Directing Council of PAHO

items.article_text_original: At the opening of the 63rd Directing Council, Dr. Jarbas Barbosa highlighted the Region’s public health gains, called for stronger regional cooperation, and underscored priorities including primary health care, vaccination, digital health and emergency preparedness. Washington, D.C., September 28, 2026 (PAHO) – Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) Director Dr. Jarbas Barbosa today highlighted the progress countries across the Americas have made in areas including primary health care, immunization, digital health and disease elimination, and called for accelerated action to address persistent and emerging challenges across the Region. Speaking at the opening of the 63rd Directing Council, which brings together Ministers of Health and other senior health authorities from across the Americas in Washington, D.C., Dr. Barbosa said the Americas continue to serve as a model for other regions of the world in public health, building on more than 120 years of joint efforts to prevent disease, strengthen health systems and protect populations. The opening session of the Directing Council also featured Lisa Cummins, Minister of Health and Wellness of Barbados and outgoing President of the Directing Council; Jayanta Bhattacharya, Director of the National Institutes of Health (NIH) of the United States; Ilan Goldfajn, President of the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB); and Ambassador Steve Ferrol, Permanent Representative of Dominica and President of the Permanent Council of the Organization of American States (OAS). “In public health, success is often measured by what does not happen. There may be no dramatic headlines, but a life may be saved, a family spared, and a community protected because a disease was prevented or an outbreak contained,” he said. Dr. Barbosa highlighted the continued efforts of countries to strengthen primary health care, improve vaccination, expand digital health, prevent and control outbreaks, reduce deaths from chronic diseases, and advance disease elimination. However, he noted that the resurgence of measles is a reminder that the work is far from finished. He called for continued efforts to strengthen surveillance, vaccination and outbreak response, while accelerating progress in maternal, newborn, child and mental health and strengthening preparedness for public health emergencies. He also called for continued focus on advancing universal health and addressing critical challenges, including the persistent shortage of health workers across the Region. “This Directing Council provides a valuable opportunity to shape our collective response to these challenges and strengthen actions to improve health across the Region,” he said. “Lasting public health progress is not delivered to countries. It is built with countries. And it starts here.” Financial sustainability of PAHO Dr. Barbosa also drew attention to the Organization’s financial sustainability and the importance of timely and full payment of assessed contributions by Member States. He recalled that Member States approved a 19% budget reduction last year and noted that, despite prioritization efforts, cost-containment measures and the strong mobilization of additional voluntary contributions, PAHO continues to face a funding gap for its core programs. “This is not simply a budgetary challenge. It affects our ability to provide technical cooperation, respond to emerging health threats, and sustain essential operations across the Region,” he said. The PAHO Director thanked the 31 Member States that have already made full or partial payments in 2026 and called on all countries to complete their contributions as soon as possible. He also thanked partners and donors for their support in advancing the Region’s health priorities. Dr. Barbosa also highlighted the value of partnerships with development banks, foundations and other strategic partners in advancing regional priorities such as digital transformation and strengthening primary health care. Key issues before the 63rd Directing Council During the week, Member States will consider new strategies and action plans to strengthen public health in the Region, including measures related to health security and emergency management, antimicrobial resistance, and the prevention and control of arboviral diseases. They will also consider a proposal to strengthen and harmonize PAHO’s Regional Revolving Funds, one of the Region’s key cooperation mechanisms for facilitating access to vaccines, medicines and other health technologies. In addition, Member States will review the results of the 2020–2025 Strategic Plan and other matters related to the Organization’s priorities and governance. At the conclusion of his remarks, Dr. Barbosa recalled that PAHO was founded on the conviction that the countries of the Americas are stronger when they work together, and called for continued innovation and cooperation to address the Region’s health challenges. “And if there is one thing the history of public health in the Americas has taught us, it is that when we work together, we can make what seems impossible today a reality,” he concluded. Quotes from other speakers at the opening session Lisa Cummins, Minister of Health and Wellness of Barbados and outgoing President of the Directing Council: “PAHO is shared infrastructure for the Americas. We must fund it. We must invest in it. And we must protect it as such. We know what happens when that infrastructure is strong: a country facing an outbreak can draw on regional surveillance and expertise; a small health system can access medicines, technical support and training that it could not readily build up alone; and research conducted in one part of our Region can help save lives in another. The measure of regional solidarity and hemispheric capacity is when we build it together and keep it ready for the people who will need it.” Jayanta Bhattacharya, Director of the National Institutes of Health (NIH): “The United States is reestablishing leadership in the Western Hemisphere. In health, that means working with countries across the Americas to build a stronger, healthier, and more resilient region, one better equipped to prevent disease, confront health threats close to their source, strengthen critical supply chains, and protect the health and security of our people. The United States is committed to extending investments and commercial partnerships across the Western Hemisphere, including sectors such as pharmaceuticals, medical devices, and food systems.” Ambassador Steve Ferrol, Permanent Representative of Dominica and President of the Permanent Council of the Organization of American States (OAS): “Ensuring that people can access essential health services is therefore not only a public health responsibility; it is an essential part of building resilient, secure, and prosperous societies. This is why health belongs at the center of our collective agenda in the Americas. Health policy and foreign policy are no longer separate conversations. The OAS stands ready to work with PAHO and with every Member State to advance this agenda.” Ilan Goldfajn, President of the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB): “The Americas face significant health challenges, including population aging, a growing burden of chronic and infectious diseases, persistent inequities in access to care, and limited public financing. No institution can address these challenges alone. That’s why our partnership with PAHO matters. PAHO brings technical leadership and a strong presence on the ground, while the IDB brings its capacity to mobilize financing and support reforms. Today, I want to highlight three areas where this cooperation can make a difference: primary health care, digital transformation, and access to medicines.” About the Directing Council The Directing Council is one of the governing bodies of the Pan American Health Organization. It brings together health authorities from Member States to set policies, approve strategies and strengthen regional health cooperation. Public sessions can be followed online through the PAHO governance portal.

items.article_text_original: At UNGA, Burundi and Guyana joined PAHO and Africa CDC to advance country-led cooperation and financing for pandemic prevention, preparedness and response Addis Ababa, New York, 22 September 2026 (PAHO/WHO, Africa CDC) – The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), together with countries and partners from Africa and the Americas, called for sustained investment in pandemic prevention, preparedness and response (PPPR), alongside stronger cooperation between the two regions to protect lives, economies and societies from future pandemics and public health emergencies. The call came at “Two Regions, One Future: Financing Pandemic Prevention, Preparedness and Response to Build Global Health Security,” a high-level side event during the 81st United Nations General Assembly, organized by the Co-operative Republic of Guyana and the Republic of Burundi, in collaboration with PAHO and Africa CDC with support from the United Nations Foundation. The event brought together leaders and partners from Africa and the Americas to examine how country-led priorities, stronger regional capacities and sustained financing can reinforce preparedness and build more resilient health systems. “The pandemic showed what happens when countries depend too heavily on distant sources for essential medicines, vaccines, diagnostics and protective equipment,” said Dr. Mohamed Irfaan Ali, President of Guyana. “Science should know north or south but access to its fruits must never depend on geography. We must build a world in which the global south has the scientific capacity, not simply to receive life-saving innovation but help create it.” “Preparedness is not a cost we pay during an emergency. It is an investment we make before one strikes – an investment in public health, certainly, but equally in our economic resilience, our social stability and our collective security,” added PAHO Director, Dr. Jarbas Barbosa. “We already have the diagnostic tools, the risk assessments, and the action plans. The real challenged is sustained financing. We must translate priorities into predictable, long-term investments – nationally, regionally, and globally – and maintain those investments during the quiet periods between crises.” Discussions drew on lessons from COVID-19 and recent infectious disease outbreaks, highlighting priorities including disease surveillance and epidemic intelligence, laboratory and genomic surveillance, early warning and rapid response, emergency coordination, and other core preparedness capacities. Sustained investment in these areas can help countries prevent, detect and contain pathogens with epidemic and pandemic potential while protecting essential health services and limiting wider social and economic disruption. “The next pandemic will not wait for the world to mobilize after a crisis begins. We must invest before emergencies strike, with countries setting the priorities and strong regional institutions able to act quickly. Africa and the Americas carry immense experience, scientific expertise and response capacity. By connecting these strengths, sharing knowledge and building predictable financing around country priorities, we can strengthen health security across both regions and contribute to a safer world,” said Dr. Jean Kaseya, Director-General of Africa CDC. Participants emphasized the importance of keeping countries at the centre of pandemic preparedness, with governments defining priorities and directing investments according to their national risks, needs and capacities. Regional organizations such as PAHO and Africa CDC can reinforce these nationally led efforts through technical cooperation, cross-border coordination, knowledge exchange and regional public goods. “The current ebola epidemic in the DRC reminds us forcefully in the urgency of investing in preparation and pandemic response,” added Ambassador Zephyrine Manirataganda, Permanent Representative of Burundi to the United Nations. “Our nation, and the nations of south America and the Caribbean face similar structural threats and we welcome south-south cooperation between our regions in terms of health preparation.” The event also called for a shift from crisis-driven funding towards sustained and strategic investment in preparedness. Such investment protects health, strengthens economic resilience and national security, and supports sustainable development. The discussion advanced a shared agenda for stronger Africa–Americas cooperation, connecting national priorities with regional capacities and more coordinated domestic, regional and global financing for health security and preparedness. “No country can build alone: The regional infrastructure that makes national preparedness coherent; surveillance networks that cross borders; laboratory systems that share capacity; emergency workers that can move where they are needed - these are collective goods, and they require collective investment,” concluded Dr. Anne-Claire Amprou, French Ambassador for Global Health and moderator of the event. The event took place ahead of the Second United Nations High-Level Meeting on Pandemic Prevention, Preparedness and Response, scheduled for September 25, where world leaders will review progress since the first meeting in 2023, and discuss how to sustain political commitment and financing for pandemic preparedness in an increasingly constrained global funding environment. Discussions also came as countries advance implementation of the WHO Pandemic Agreement and other global commitments aimed at strengthening health emergency preparedness and response.
